segments.text: When we feed text into an artificial intelligence, the system breaks those words down into tokens and assigns each one a unique numerical ID.
But that number is strictly an organizational tool.
It contains absolutely zero information about what the token actually means.
Think about it like a school setting. An ID identifies you. It doesn't describe you.
The badge is perfectly identify which student is which, but they tell us absolutely nothing about who each person is.
His ID number won't tell you he's the one who steals fries.
The same logic applies to an AI's vocabulary.
Assigning a token ID is a required first step, but a number alone is not enough for the system to process meaning.
To give a system that context, we need a way to quantify characteristics.
Imagine we are running a simple taste test. We decide to rate Coke and coffee across six distinct characteristics.
Sweet, bitter, fizz, heat, caffeine, and dark, using a scale where zero is low and ten is high.
This table captures our ratings for the two drinks.
Looking at the first row for Coke, we rate it a nine for sweet, one for bitter, ten for fizz, two for heat, three for caffeine, and eight for dark.
Moving down to the next row, coffee gets a completely different set of scores.
Each position always means the same thing. The number says how much.
If I cover up the names and ask you which drink scores a nine for sweet, a one for bitter, and a ten for fizz, you immediately know the answer.
It's Coke. In formal AI terminology, the whole row of numbers is a vector.
Each individual position in that row is a dimension, and the specific number placed inside it is its value.
This updated table shows what happens when we add a third drink to our test, Pepsi.
If we rate it across our existing six dimensions, we run into a problem. Pepsi scores exactly the same as Coke.
Relying on these six numbers alone, we cannot tell them apart.
To fix this, we simply add a seventh dimension to the far right side of the board, Citrus.
Now we score Pepsi a ten on Citrus, while Coke scores a one, and coffee scores a zero.
Six numbers match. The seventh tells them apart.
When meanings are highly similar, adding more dimensions allows us to separate them and capture the subtle differences.
This comparison chart maps our simple taste test directly to how AI models process language.
An artificial intelligence also uses rows of numbers to represent meaning.
That row is called an embedding.
Instead of assigning a row to just three drinks, the AI assigns one to every single token in its entire vocabulary.
And instead of maxing out at six or seven dimensions, an AI model typically uses thousands.
Rather than a human choosing ratings from zero to ten, the AI learns its values during training, filling those dimensions with positive and negative numbers, including complex decimals.
We explicitly named our traits, like sweet or fizz.
An AI has no dimension labels at all.
They simply capture patterns in how a token is used in data.
Both use a row of numbers to describe something.
We use it to quantify flavor, and the AI uses it to map out the structure of language.
Let's see this inside an actual model architecture.
When we input the word cat, the system identifies its token ID as 4719.
It follows that ID directly to the embedding table.
It stores one embedding for every single token, meaning cat sits right alongside rows for dog, latte, truck, and bicycle.
The first two columns list the token ID and the token itself.
Everything to the right represents the dimensions marked D1 through Dn.
Each individual learned number in this sequence, like that 0.45, is called a parameter.
The complete continuous row of those numbers forms the embedding.
The system is so thorough that even word fragments get this treatment.
If a word like unbelievable is split into pieces like Unbelie and Vable,
every one of those gets its own dedicated row of learned numbers in the table.
AI uses numbers to work with meaning.
Those numbers help AI recognize similarities and differences.
